solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Do their victims leave them deflated, figuratively and literally? (7,8)

annotation.definition: Do their victims leave them deflated, figuratively and literally?

blocks.clueFragment: Do their victims leave them deflated
blocks.note: the surface reading: people bullied or pranked are left feeling flat; the setter means the victim's weight squashes the thing flat
both senses at once: the prank's target is embarrassed, and the rubber prop loses its air

annotation.surface: A question about bullies and the sorry state of those they pick on.
annotation.walkthrough: The victim sits down and squashes the cushion flat (literally deflated), and is left red-faced by the rude noise (figuratively deflated).
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: sitting on the rubber prank cushion flattens it, and the rude noise flattens the sitter's dignity.

entries.clue: Site managers grasp spades beneath netting (10)

indicatorNotes.beneath: in a down answer, what comes beneath is written after, so WEB goes on top

blocks.note: to grasp a skill is to master it

annotation.surface: Builders' foremen with shovels, standing under safety netting on a building site.
annotation.walkthrough: The 'site' is a website, not a building site; the spades and netting make it look like construction.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: webmasters are the people who run websites, the online sense of 'site'.

entries.clue: Where finger is ready for action? Exactly (2,3,6)

annotation.definition: Where finger is ready for action?

blocks.clueFragment: Where finger is ready for action?
blocks.note: picture a finger resting on the switch of a doorbell or detonator
an idiom for precisely, spot on, as in arriving at noon sharp

annotation.surface: Someone poised to act, then a one-word confirmation.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half is a cryptic picture of a finger resting on a button; the second is the idiom's plain meaning.
annotation.definitionFit: Both halves are idioms: a finger resting on a push-switch, and the phrase for precise timing or accuracy, as in 'noon on the button'.

entries.clue: Conditions favouring five pit stops periodically (8)

indicatorNotes.periodically: periodically means at regular intervals, so every second letter is taken

blocks.note: V is the Roman numeral for five
p-I-t-S-t-O-p-S: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

annotation.surface: Motor racing: track conditions that suit a strategy of five pit stops.
annotation.walkthrough: The Formula One picture hides that 'Conditions' means terms in a contract.
annotation.definitionFit: A legal-drafting synonym: a proviso is a condition written into an agreement.

entries.clue: Writer says it’s ridiculous to support English (8)

indicatorNotes.ridiculous: the letters are made absurd, i.e. rearranged
indicatorNotes.to support: in a down answer, the supporting piece sits underneath, so it follows E

annotation.surface: An author dismisses something as ridiculous, backing the English side.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s of 'it's' is part of the fodder: you need all three S's.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: someone who writes essays is a kind of writer.

entries.clue: Outstanding PA in college ultimately rewarded (6)

indicatorNotes.in: PA goes inside the word for college
indicatorNotes.ultimately: ultimately means in the end, so only the end of 'rewarded', its final letter D, is used

blocks.note: taken as written, placed inside UNI

annotation.surface: A brilliant personal assistant at a college finally gets recognition.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' looks like praise for the PA, but it means still owed, as a bill is.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the money sense: an outstanding bill is one nobody has settled yet.

entries.clue: Loves suit (6)

blocks.note: loved ones, as in 'my dear' or 'sweetheart'
one of the four suits in a pack of cards, the red one with the love symbol

annotation.surface: Someone likes what they wear, or a suitor's affection.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as a sentence, 'suit' is an item of clothing or a courtship; it is the card suit.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are plain: hearts as affections or loved ones, and the card suit with the heart symbol.

entries.clue: Ticket scalper scratching head, possibly stumped (3)

indicatorNotes.scratching head: to scratch is to strike out, so scratching the head strikes out the first letter

blocks.note: a tout resells tickets at inflated prices
the head of the scalper's word is its first letter, which is scratched off

annotation.surface: A ticket scalper scratches his head, perhaps puzzled.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Scratching head' looks like the tout is baffled, which makes 'stumped' seem to mean puzzled; stumped is a way to be out in cricket, hence 'possibly'.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: being stumped is one of the ways a cricket batter can be dismissed, hence 'possibly'.

entries.clue: Dress right when going around India (4)

indicatorNotes.going around: turn the pieces back to front

blocks.note: India is I in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Advice to dress properly when travelling round India.
annotation.walkthrough: India turns up in the surface as the sari's home country, but here it only supplies I.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the sari is a draped garment worn in South Asia, one kind of dress.

entries.clue: Cheers sitcom’s over (7,2)

blocks.note: Bottom's: Bottom was a BBC sitcom with Rik Mayall and Ade Edmondson

annotation.surface: Cheers, the American sitcom, has ended its run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' is itself the name of a sitcom, which makes it look like part of the wordplay; it is the toast, and the sitcom is Bottom, a 1990s BBC comedy.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'Bottoms up!' and 'Cheers!' are both toasts said before drinking.

entries.clue: Statute meeting zero resistance in Washington, for example (5)

indicatorNotes.meeting: the pieces are joined up side by side

annotation.surface: A law passing in the US capital with no opposition.
annotation.walkthrough: Washington looks like the city where laws are passed; it is Denzel Washington, the actor.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Denzel Washington works in film, so his surname stands for anyone in his profession.

entries.clue: Service‘s last word, with one extremely teary (7)

indicatorNotes.extremely: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so extremely teary keeps just T and Y

blocks.note: amen is the last word of a prayer
T and Y, the ends of teary

annotation.surface: A church service ends with the final amen and one mourner in tears.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Service' looks like a church service, which feeds AMEN, but it is the definition: an amenity is a facility or service.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a hotel's gym or pool is an amenity, a service provided for guests.

entries.clue: In time cuddles moggy returning uninjured (6)

indicatorNotes.cuddles: wraps around, so the cat goes inside

blocks.note: moggy is British slang for a cat

annotation.surface: A cat comes home safe and gets a cuddle just in time.
annotation.walkthrough: IN and T together hold the reversed cat between them.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something intact is unharmed, whole, with nothing broken.

entries.clue: Mad spy’s timepiece (6,5)

blocks.note: to clock someone is to notice or spot them

annotation.surface: A crazed secret agent's watch.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spy' is a verb, to catch sight of, not a secret agent; to clock something is British slang for noticing it.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a cuckoo clock is a timepiece in which a toy bird calls the hours.

entries.clue: Lord Peter Wimsey’s latest suspect, allegedly (10)

indicatorNotes.latest: the latest thing comes last, so the latest of Wimsey is its final letter
indicatorNotes.suspect: as an adjective suspect means dubious, not to be trusted as it stands, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Dorothy L Sayers' sleuth Lord Peter Wimsey has named his newest suspect, so they say.
annotation.walkthrough: Lord Peter Wimsey is Dorothy L Sayers' aristocratic detective, so 'suspect' reads as a noun; it is the anagram indicator.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: 'reportedly' and 'allegedly' both mean according to what people say, unconfirmed.

entries.clue: Bad egg at the end of short trip somewhere in France (8)

indicatorNotes.short: something short falls short of its full length, so TOUR loses its last letter
indicatorNotes.at the end of: LOUSE is placed at the end of the trip, i.e. after TOU

blocks.note: a louse is a contemptible person

annotation.surface: A rotten egg eaten at the end of a short holiday in France.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bad egg' sounds like food poisoning abroad; it is old slang for a rotter, a louse.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Toulouse is a city in south-west France, one of many places there.

entries.clue: High point from Requiem Carreras recalled (4)

indicatorNotes.from: the answer comes from within the words that follow, sitting inside them
indicatorNotes.recalled: to recall is to call back, so the letters are read backwards

annotation.surface: The tenor José Carreras's Requiem performance remembered as a career peak.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer runs backwards across the join between the two words.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the acme of something is its peak or pinnacle.

entries.clue: Dawn: reddish-brown duck observed by Spooner (8)

indicatorNotes.observed by Spooner: Rev William Spooner famously swapped the starts of words, so what he would say is the sound-swapped version

blocks.note: bay is a reddish-brown horse colour
a drake is a male duck
swap the opening sounds of the two words, then respell as one word

annotation.surface: Someone called Dawn spots a reddish-brown duck.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dawn' at the front with a colon looks like a name introducing a scene; it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: daybreak and dawn are both the first light of morning.

entries.clue: A reprint ordered for The Swimmer (8)

indicatorNotes.ordered: to order things is to arrange them, so the letters are arranged afresh

annotation.surface: A publisher orders a reprint of The Swimmer, John Cheever's story.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Swimmer' looks like a book title needing a reprint; it is simply something that swims.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic example: a terrapin is a freshwater turtle, and the capitalised title disguises a simple description of a swimming creature.

entries.clue: Pets for some celebrity from the east (4)

indicatorNotes.from the east: an across answer reads west to east, so going from the east means reading right to left

annotation.surface: A celebrity's pets, perhaps imported from the Far East.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For some' hedges the definition: not everyone keeps rats, but some people do.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: fancy rats are kept as pets, but only by some people, hence the hedge.

entries.clue: Some Italian water and fizzy cola, OK with me (4,4)

indicatorNotes.fizzy: fizzy means bubbling and agitated, so the letters are stirred up

annotation.surface: Ordering drinks in Italy: some mineral water and a fizzy cola will do for me.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Italian water' reads as bottled San Pellegrino; it is a whole lake.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Lake Como in Lombardy is one body of Italian water among many.

entries.clue: Santa’s reindeer – deer oddly ignored? (6)

indicatorNotes.oddly ignored: the odd-numbered letters, first and third, are ignored, leaving the second and fourth

blocks.note: the punctuation mark in the clue is a dash
dEeR without its odd letters D and E

annotation.surface: A reindeer named, then a quibble that one should skip the word 'deer'.
annotation.walkthrough: The dash looks like mere punctuation, but it is a piece of wordplay: the symbol itself is a DASH.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Dasher is the first of Santa's reindeer named in the poem 'A Visit from St Nicholas'.

entries.clue: Player’s quick break during pressure over (6)

indicatorNotes.during: something during another thing happens within it, so REST goes inside P…O

annotation.surface: A sportsman grabs a brief rest when under pressure at the end of the over.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Player' is a musician, not a sportsman; presto is a tempo marking telling them to play quickly.
annotation.definitionFit: A specialist sense: presto is the tempo marking telling a musician to play very fast.

entries.clue: Biased newspaper rejecting small fine (6)

indicatorNotes.rejecting: to reject is to throw out, so the S for small is thrown out of SUN

blocks.note: the Sun, a British tabloid, rejecting S

annotation.surface: A partisan paper throws out a minor penalty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fine' looks like a penalty to be rejected; it means fair, as weather is. The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a biased referee or judgment is an unfair one.

entries.clue: Before start of term, find only half of boring school soup (7)

indicatorNotes.only half of: only half of a six-letter word keeps three letters, here the first three
indicatorNotes.start of: the start of a word is its first letter, so the start of term is T
indicatorNotes.Before: what is named 'before' comes first, so BOR and SCH go ahead of T

blocks.note: SCH is a standard abbreviation for school

annotation.surface: A pupil complains about dull school soup at the start of term.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue names term first, but 'before' means the pieces from boring and school come ahead of it. SCH is the standard dictionary abbreviation for school.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: borscht is an Eastern European beetroot soup.

entries.clue: List of courses Mickelson enjoyed naming, usually at the front every time (4)

indicatorNotes.at the front every time: each word's front is its first letter, and every time means take one from each word

annotation.surface: Golfer Phil Mickelson liked listing the golf courses he played, usually leading the field.
annotation.walkthrough: Mickelson is a golfer, so 'courses' reads as golf courses; they are the courses of a meal.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the dining sense: a menu is the list of dishes, the courses a restaurant offers.

entries.clue: Planet‘s craft – what controls it? (5)

indicatorNotes.controls: to control something is to hold it in check, so EH holds ART inside

annotation.surface: A question about who steers a spaceship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It' points back to the craft: EH holds ART.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Earth is one of the planets of the solar system, the third from the Sun.

entries.clue: Maybe Stewart Granger finally departs holding Oscar (3)

indicatorNotes.finally: finally means at the end, so only the last letter of Granger, R, is used
indicatorNotes.holding: R and D hold O between them, like hands gripping it

blocks.note: Oscar is O in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: The film star Stewart Granger leaves clutching an Academy Award.
annotation.walkthrough: Stewart Granger was a film actor, so the two names look fused; the definition is 'Maybe Stewart', as in the singer Rod Stewart. R and D hold O between them.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: Rod is a first name, and the singer Rod Stewart shows Stewart can go with it, hence 'Maybe'.

entries.clue: Pen second Dickensian character, female past her time (9)

blocks.note: Uriah Heep, the creep in David Copperfield

annotation.surface: A writer's second-rate Dickens pastiche featuring an ageing woman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pen' looks like writing, which suits Dickens; it is an animal enclosure.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the farming sense: a pen is an enclosure for animals, and a sheepfold is the one for sheep.

entries.clue: Where player might be in collapsed scrum, yanked about? Shut up! (5,4,3,3)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around in all directions, so the letters are moved around

blocks.clueFragment: Where player might be in collapsed scrum
blocks.note: a lock is a rugby forward, who might end up under the pile

annotation.surface: A rugby player trapped at the bottom of a collapsed scrum, pulled out and told to be quiet.
annotation.walkthrough: In rugby union the locks are the two second-row forwards; a player crushed at the bottom of the scrum could be under a lock. 'Shut up!' means locked away, not be quiet.
annotation.definitionFit: Under lock and key means securely shut up, as in prison.
